blocks.prompt: The Egg That Builds a Bird
blocks.text: An egg looks simple, but it is a little house. The hard shell is the wall. The clear part is called the white. The yellow part is called the yolk. If a hen sits on the egg and keeps it warm, a chick grows inside. It eats the yolk while it grows. It takes twenty one days. When the chick is ready, it has a tiny hard bump on its beak. The bump is called an egg tooth. The chick taps the shell with it, again and again, until the shell breaks. Then the egg tooth falls off. The chick does not need it anymore.

blocks.prompt: The Strongest Thing in Your Kitchen
blocks.text: An egg looks fragile. Tap it on the side of a bowl and it cracks right open. But hold an egg the long way, with one end in your palm and the other end under your fingers, and squeeze as hard as you can. Most people cannot break it. The egg is not weak. It is shaped like an arch. An arch spreads a push out along its curve instead of letting it pile up in one spot. Builders have used arches in bridges and doorways for thousands of years. The egg got there first. The shell has another surprise. It is not solid. It is covered in thousands of tiny holes called pores, far too small to see. Air moves in through them, and water moves out. That matters, because a chick growing inside the shell needs to breathe. The shell keeps the chick safe and lets it breathe at the same time.

blocks.prompt: Why a Fried Egg Cannot Go Back
blocks.text: Crack a raw egg into a pan and you get a puddle. Leave it over heat for two minutes and the puddle turns white and firm. Nothing was added. Nothing was taken away. So what changed? The answer is protein. Egg white is about nine tenths water. Almost all the rest is protein, and each protein is a long chain folded up tight into a little ball, tucked into the water like a wound spring. Heat makes those chains jiggle. Jiggle them enough and the folds shake loose. The chains uncurl, bump into their neighbors, and grab hold. Soon they are linked into a mesh that traps the water between them. Liquid becomes solid. Scientists call that unfolding step denaturing. Here is the part that surprises people. You cannot undo it. Cool a fried egg down and it stays a fried egg forever. The chains cannot refold the way they were. That is why cooking an egg is a one way trip, and why a burned egg cannot be rescued. There is one more clue hiding in your kitchen. Drop an egg into a glass of water. A fresh egg sinks and lies flat. An old egg tips up, or floats. Every egg holds a small pocket of air inside its blunt end, and that pocket grows as water slowly escapes through the shell. The more air, the higher the egg rides. The glass of water is telling you how old the egg is.

answers: they unfold, link to each other, and trap the water in a mesh
(the chains cannot refold into their original shape)

(inference: it sets up a puzzle, since the change must come from inside the egg)

blocks.prompt: The Shell Factory, and an Argument About Shape
blocks.text: Every hen builds her eggs one at a time, and the whole job takes about a day. The yolk comes first, released from the ovary. As it travels down a long tube called the oviduct, layer after layer is added around it: the thick white, then thin membranes, and finally the shell itself, which is laid down over roughly twenty hours in a chamber near the end. The shell is almost pure calcium carbonate, the same mineral as chalk and limestone. A hen laying an egg a day is spending a startling amount of calcium, which is why laying hens are fed crushed shell and grit. Now the harder question: why is an egg egg-shaped? Not a ball, not a tube. Every egg is a dome at each end, and a dome is one of the strongest shapes known. Press on a dome and the force runs outward along the curve instead of piling up in one place. A hen settles on her clutch with her full weight, and the eggs hold. Yet a chick can break out from the inside, because pushing outward on a dome is far easier than pushing inward. Different birds lay different shapes, and one of those shapes started an argument that lasted a century. The common murre nests on bare cliff ledges with no nest at all, and its egg is dramatically pointed, like a pear. For decades, textbooks explained that a pointed egg rolls in a tight circle rather than rolling off the cliff. It is a tidy story. When researchers finally tested it carefully, the tidy story wobbled. Pointed eggs do roll in an arc, but on a real sloping ledge that arc is not much protection. Newer work suggests the shape helps in other ways: a pointed egg sits more steadily when it is tilted, and it keeps the blunt end, where the chick's air pocket forms, lifted away from the dirt. The argument is not settled, which is the honest state of a great deal of science.

6.title: The Egg That Builds a Bird
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Egg That Builds a Bird

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Shell about 0.3 mm thick, roughly 95% calcium carbonate
Thousands of pores, capped by a coating called the cuticle
The US washes eggs; much of Europe bans washing
Two cords called chalazae hold the yolk centered
The chick takes calcium out of the shell for its bones
A bee hummingbird egg is about the size of a pea

blocks.prompt: Sealed at the Factory: The Engineering of an Egg
blocks.text: Consider the problem an egg has to solve. A bird must build a complete chick from scratch outside its own body. The chick needs food, water, air, warmth, protection from crushing, protection from bacteria, and somewhere to put its waste. All of it must be sealed inside a container before the bird ever lays it, because after that no delivery is possible. The chick that emerges three weeks later is built entirely from what was packed in on day one. There is no resupply. Start with the container. A chicken shell is about a third of a millimeter thick and roughly ninety five percent calcium carbonate, the mineral of chalk and limestone. On its own, calcium carbonate is unremarkable stuff. The shell's strength comes from geometry, not material. Each end is a dome, and a dome turns a push into compression spread along a curve. Squeeze an egg end to end in your palm and most adults cannot break it. Yet the same shell yields to a hatching chick, because a dome is far weaker from the inside than from the outside. The egg is deliberately strong in one direction and weak in the other. The shell also has to breathe. A developing chick burns oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, so the shell is drilled with thousands of microscopic pores, each far too small to see. Air passes through them freely. So, unfortunately, does anything else small enough. The bird's answer is a thin protein coating called the cuticle, or bloom, applied last, just before laying. It caps the pore openings against bacteria while still letting gas trade back and forth. That coating explains an argument between two continents. In the United States, eggs are washed at the packing plant, which strips the cuticle away, so they must be refrigerated from that moment until they are cracked. In much of Europe, washing is banned for exactly the same reason: leave the cuticle in place and the egg protects itself on the counter. Two food safety systems, opposite rules, both defensible, each one sensible only inside its own logic. Inside the shell, the packing is just as careful. Two twisted white cords called the chalazae anchor the yolk in the middle, cushioned no matter how the egg is turned. The yolk is the food. The white is the water supply and a shock absorber. As water slips out through the pores, a pocket of air grows at the blunt end, and in the last day before hatching the chick pushes its beak into that pocket and takes its first real breath while still sealed inside. Then it begins tapping with a hard point on its beak called the egg tooth, which drops off once the job is done. The final detail is the strangest. A chick needs calcium for its skeleton, and no calcium is coming in. So it takes what it needs from the shell, dissolving the inside surface as it grows. The wall of the room becomes the bones of the animal in the room, and the shell the chick finally breaks is thinner than the one it started in, because it has been eating it.
